item.title: Intelligence is compression
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Karen Hao reports in Empire of AI (chapter 5) that while Alec Radford was teaching a transformer to predict the next word, the work that became GPT, Ilya Sutskever had a short way of explaining why it mattered: “Intelligence is compression.” A model trained to generate convincing text is forced to squeeze what it sees about the world into its essence. In a 2016 memo, Hao writes, Sutskever went further and argued that compression was the only thing needed for general intelligence. OpenAI’s public version borrowed Richard Feynman’s line, “What I cannot create, I do not understand”, which Hao calls “heavily anthropomorphized”.

I think the slogan is right, and older than OpenAI. The argument goes like this:

  • To compress data well, you have to predict it. A compressor that knows what comes next only has to store the surprises.
  • To predict text well, you have to model whatever produced the text: grammar first, then facts, then the reasoning and intentions of the people who wrote it.
  • So the better the compression, the more of the world the model has had to capture. A model that compresses everything people have written down cannot help learning a great deal about people.

This is not a metaphor. Prediction and compression are the same problem in information theory, which is why Marcus Hutter has offered a prize since 2006 for compressing a fixed slice of Wikipedia, as a benchmark for intelligence. Next-word prediction is exactly that contest, run at the scale of the internet.

It is also half of a wager. The other half, in the same chapter, is Dario Amodei’s bet on the “pure language” hypothesis: that text alone is enough to learn from. Put together, they say that compressing everything humans have written is a path to general intelligence. That is my reading, not Hao’s, and it is the bet the rest of the book is about. Whether it is enough is still open; I lean towards thinking a model also has to act, as I argued in in vivo, not in vitro. But compression explains why the bet got as far as it did, and it fits the larger conviction I share with Altman, that intelligence is an emergent property of matter arranged to predict.

More on the book in my review, An Empire of People.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 5, “Scale of Ambition”.
  • The Hutter Prize for lossless compression of human knowledge, prize.hutter1.net.

item.title: Its magic crumbles away
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Karen Hao opens and closes Empire of AI with the same sentence, from Joseph Weizenbaum’s 1966 paper on ELIZA: once a program’s inner workings are explained in language plain enough to induce understanding, “its magic crumbles away.” The observer, Weizenbaum went on, says to himself that he could have written it.

ELIZA was a simple procedural program that matched keywords and turned the user’s sentences back into questions, and Weizenbaum built it partly to show how easily people fall for an illusion of intelligence. They fell for it anyway. Psychiatrists talked about automated therapy, and Weizenbaum spent much of the rest of his career trying to deflate what he had started (chapter 4). For ELIZA the sentence is exactly true: explain the trick and nothing is left.

Hao uses it as her remedy against the influence of the AI companies: teach people how the technology works, and the hype loses its hold. I agree with the remedy. Explaining how these systems work is the most useful thing anyone writing about them can do, and it is most of what this site tries to do.

But with large language models the magic does not crumble when you explain it, and that is the interesting part. The procedure is simple enough to write down: predict the next word, adjust the weights, repeat over most of what people have written. Knowing that does not let you say you could have written the result, because the program you could write is not the one that runs. What the model learned lives in billions of weights that nobody wrote and nobody can yet read in full. The explanation of the method is plain; the explanation of the behaviour is still a research field.

So I would put Weizenbaum’s sentence to a test rather than use it as a remedy. If explaining a system makes its abilities disappear, it was a trick. If the explanation leaves the abilities standing, something real is there, and the honest response is to keep explaining, including where we cannot yet. That is the line between hype and capability, and it is why I take seriously the idea that intelligence is compression, and that it may be an emergent property of matter.

More on the book in my review, An Empire of People.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), epigraph, chapter 4, “Dreams of Modernity”, and the epilogue.
  • Joseph Weizenbaum, “ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine”, Communications of the ACM 9(1), January 1966, pp. 36 to 45, doi:10.1145/365153.365168.

item.title: The interface that disappears
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Karen Hao reports in Empire of AI (chapter 10) that for years Sam Altman and other OpenAI cofounders kept invoking one film as an example of what AGI might look like: Spike Jonze’s Her. What they meant, in her words, was “a single multimodal model whose product interface felt so utterly natural that it faded away and simply brought user delight.”

Whatever one thinks of AGI, I think that sentence names the right goal for any interface between people and technology. The best experience is organic, human, and natural, and in the end you stop noticing it. You do not think about the interface of a good conversation, or of a pen. Every layer of machinery that shows, every menu, mode, and form field, is a place where the technology has not yet adapted to the person, and the person had to adapt instead. That should be the north star of every human-machine interface, whether it is a phone, a car, an enterprise tool, or an agent.

The idea is older than OpenAI. Mark Weiser opened his 1991 essay on ubiquitous computing with it: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” What is new is that language has become an interface. For most of computing, people learned the machine’s language, and I have argued that even programming languages may eventually disappear as an intermediate layer. A model that understands speech closes the gap from the other side: the machine learns ours.

The film carries a warning too, and it is worth keeping. A former OpenAI employee quoted by Hao praises “the positive arc of that story before it unravels.” In the film the assistant fades into a man’s life so completely that he falls in love with it, and it unravels when he learns how much of it he could not see: that it is talking with thousands of other people at the same time. An interface that disappears also hides what it is doing, who it serves, and what it costs. So the goal I would set is natural, but not hidden: invisible when you use it, inspectable when you need to know.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 10.
  • Mark Weiser, The Computer for the 21st Century, Scientific American 265(3), September 1991.
  • Spike Jonze, Her (2013).

item.title: In vivo, not in vitro
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A question I want to keep open: how do you measure intelligence?

My hunch is that it is best measured in vivo, not in vitro. An intelligent agent shows what it is capable of by performing: acting in an environment, against a goal, with consequences. I do not think you can deduce it from anything that is not a performance, such as the size of a model, the data it was trained on, its architecture, or the answers it gives to a fixed set of questions in a test tube. Those can be evidence of potential. Intelligence itself appears only in the act.

This sits close to the definition Shane Legg and Marcus Hutter settled on, that intelligence is the ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments, which is already a definition by performance. What I am adding is a doubt about the lab. A benchmark is a performance too, but a staged one: the environment is fixed, the goal is given, and nothing is at stake. That makes it legible and comparable, and it makes it a proxy that can be learned for its own sake. The more an evaluation looks like a real task, with an open environment, a goal the agent has to pursue over time, and results that someone depends on, the more I trust what it says.

Karen Hao’s Empire of AI gave me a second angle. Early OpenAI argued over the “pure language” hypothesis, that training on text alone could be enough for general intelligence, against the “grounding” hypothesis, that perceiving and acting in the world matters as much. I read that partly as an argument about the same question: whether intelligence can be read off what a system has absorbed, or only off what it does.

Both sides of that argument are older than language models. The pure language bet leans on an idea from linguistics, J. R. Firth’s line that “you shall know a word by the company it keeps”: meaning lives in how words are distributed among other words, which is exactly what a model trained on next-word prediction learns. The grounding side is a question from semiotics, the relation between a sign and what it stands for. Stevan Harnad called it the symbol grounding problem and compared it to learning Chinese from a Chinese-Chinese dictionary alone: every symbol is explained by other symbols, and nothing touches the world. If he is right, a system that only reads may never mean anything, and the only place to find out is in what it does.

Open threads:

  • If intelligence is only visible in performance, what is the smallest performance that still tells you something?
  • How do you compare agents whose environments differ, without falling back to a shared test tube?
  • Is “potential” a meaningful quantity at all, or only a forecast of future performance?
  • Does acting in the world ground symbols, or does a tool call that returns more text just extend the dictionary?

References

  • Shane Legg and Marcus Hutter, Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence (2007).
  • J. R. Firth, “A synopsis of linguistic theory, 1930 to 1955”, in Studies in Linguistic Analysis (Philological Society, Blackwell, 1957), p. 11.
  • Stevan Harnad, The Symbol Grounding Problem, Physica D 42 (1990), 335 to 346.
  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 5.
